rationale: A wins because it keeps the story sellable without pretending the fact sheet says more than it does. Its strongest line, "Patagonia won't say how big its resale business actually is," turns a disclosure gap into a legitimate retail-financial story; B's opener, "something no major apparel brand has attempted," walks straight into invented-superlative territory. B has usable bones, but it keeps dressing inference as fact, and reporters are paid to notice that.
gaps_in_A: "Patagonia expands a program built to sell you less clothing" leans on a business-model thesis the update does not prove; A correctly flags this later, but the headline still overstates the evidence.
"How to get Patagonia gear repaired for free" risks over-promising because only basic repairs are free; A names that caveat, but the angle headline is still a little too broad.

"whether a national chain putting free repair drop-off in 70+ stores plus mail-in is evidence the category itself has matured" needs outside market proof before it becomes a category trend, not just a Patagonia rollout.
gaps_in_B: "something no major apparel brand has attempted" is an invented first/only claim. The update gives Patagonia facts, not a competitive audit.
"trained staff, parts logistics, and turnaround management at a scale no comparable US apparel brand has matched" smuggles in operational facts and a market comparison the update does not provide.
"no publicly traded apparel company could defend to shareholders" is sweeping and unsupported. It sounds clever until a reporter asks for proof.
"shorten its own sales pipeline" is jargon dressed as strategy, and it muddles the actual tension: repair may reduce new-unit purchases, but the update does not prove that behavior.
